import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Green's Open Problem 28

References:
- [Green, Ben. "100 open problems." (2024).](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#problem.28)
- [Mathoverflow/339137](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339137/why-do-polynomials-with-coefficients-0-1-like-to-have-only-factors-with-0-1) asked by user [Sil](https://mathoverflow.net/users/136794/sil)
- [MathStackexchange/3325163](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3325163/) asked by user [Emmanuel Amiot](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/403309/emmanuel-amiot)
-/

namespace Green28

/-- True if a PMF on $\mathbb{Z}$ is uniformly distributed on its support. -/
def IsUniformOnSupport (X : PMF ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∃ (s : Finset ℤ) (hs : s.Nonempty), X = PMF.uniformOfFinset s hs

/--
The discrete convolution of two PMFs on $\mathbb{Z}$, representing the distribution of the sum of
two independent random variables.
-/
noncomputable def indepSum (X Y : PMF ℤ) : PMF ℤ := do
  let x ← X
  let y ← Y
  PMF.pure (x + y)

/--
Suppose that $X, Y$ are two finitely-supported independent random variables taking integer values,
and such that $X + Y$ is uniformly distributed on its range. Are $X$ and $Y$ themselves uniformly
distributed on their ranges?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 60]
theorem green_28 : answer(sorry) ↔
  ∀ (X Y : PMF ℤ), -- marginals, independence is built into indepSum
    X.support.Finite ∧ Y.support.Finite ∧ IsUniformOnSupport (indepSum X Y) →
      IsUniformOnSupport X ∧ IsUniformOnSupport Y := by
  sorry

end Green28

reformulations.difference: The theorem quantifies over marginal PMFs, encoding independence through convolution rather than an explicit independence hypothesis. The original MSE problem instead uses monic nonnegative real polynomial factors.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An independent pair with marginal masses p and q has sum law z ↦ ∑' x, p(x)q(z−x), which is exactly indepSum (this identity was proved in the scratch file). Conversely, any pair of PMFs is realized independently by the coordinate functions on the product probability space. Finite support and uniformity depend only on the laws, so the PMF and random-variable formulations are equivalent. For the polynomial formulation, translate the finite integer supports into the natural numbers and form probability-generating polynomials. Dividing each by its positive leading coefficient makes it monic; when the convolution is uniform, their product has coefficients 0 or 1. Conversely, dividing monic nonnegative polynomial factors by their positive values at 1 gives PMFs. Constant nonzero coefficients correspond precisely to uniform distributions.

review.notes: All three declarations were checked; no mathematical or status defects were found. The consulted sources still record the general problem as open. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles successfully without sorry-dependent proofs. It proves the uniformity characterization, convolution formula, and support-sumset identity; checks nonempty supports and point-mass boundary cases; verifies that uniforms on {0,1} and {0,2} have uniform sum on {0,1,2,3}; and verifies that two independent uniforms on {0,1} instead have unequal masses 1/4 and 1/2 at 0 and 1. The full random-variable/polynomial equivalence was checked mathematically, not formalized as a Lean biconditional.
